records.quote: Valentin behind his tree was tearing his fingernails with silent fury.
records.paraphrase: Valentin reacts with frustration while overhearing what seems to be innocent theological talk.

records.quote: "Pray excuse my apparent irrelevance, my good sir, but I should like to ask you a question in experimental psychology and the association of ideas."
records.paraphrase: Valentin frames his questioning of the fruiterer as an inquiry into experimental psychology and association of ideas.

records.quote: the inspector said under his breath, "Are we after escaped lunatics?"
records.paraphrase: A detective reacts with disbelief at the seemingly senseless behavior of the men they are pursuing.

records.quote: He said that if one had a clue this was the worst way; but if one had no clue at all it was the best, because there was just the chance that any oddity that caught the eye of the pursuer might be the same that had caught the eye of the pursued.
records.paraphrase: Valentin explains his method of following the unreasonable when no clue exists, reasoning that oddities noticed by pursuer and pursued may coincide.

records.quote: There was nothing about him to indicate the fact that the grey jacket covered a loaded revolver, that the white waistcoat covered a police card, or that the straw hat covered one of the most powerful intellects in Europe.
records.paraphrase: The narrator contrasts Valentin's ordinary holiday appearance with his concealed weapon, authority, and intellect.

records.quote: He had put salt in it.
records.paraphrase: Valentin discovers the salt swapped for sugar, prompting his investigation of the anomaly.

records.quote: He looked to see if there were any more orthodox vessels. Yes; there were two salt-cellars quite full. Perhaps there was some speciality in the condiment in the salt-cellars. He tasted it; it was sugar.
records.paraphrase: Valentin systematically tests the containers to determine that sugar and salt have been deliberately swapped.

candidate.paraphrase: Valentin lays out his tracking procedure: to mimic the movements of a target whose actions are unknown.

candidate.quote: "A man generally makes a small scene if he finds salt in his coffee; if he doesn fffffffffffffft, he has some reason for keeping quiet. I changed the salt and sugar, and you kept quiet. A man generally objects if his bill is three times too big. If he pays it, he has some motive for passing unnoticed. I altered your bill, and you paid it."
candidate.paraphrase: Father Brown explains the reasoning behind his tests: normal reactions versus suppressed ones reveal a person with something to hide.

criteria.rationale: Valentin's passing reference to 'experimental psychology and the association of ideas' is rhetorical banter, not a material representation of scientific facts, theories, or natural processes. The story is a detective tale with no genuine scientific content driving the narrative.

Devices mentioned (telescope, microscope, portable pillar-box) are ordinary contemporary tools or incidental background color from Flambeau's past exploits; no engineered system or invention materially affects the central problem, action, or outcome, which turns on trickery and deduction.
The story is set in a contemporary present with no speculative future, remote past, or temporal displacement of any kind.

The narrative does not develop consequences from an identifiable scientific, technological, social, or historical premise; it is a self-contained detective puzzle resolved by cunning, not by extrapolating a novum.

Both Valentin's method of following the unreasonable and Father Brown's deliberate testing (swapping salt/sugar, altering bills as behavioral tests) resemble systematic inference, observation, and hypothesis-testing that materially drive the action. However, this is detective reasoning rather than scientific method in a genre sense, so materiality and interpretation remain uncertain.

Talk of 'other worlds' and 'infinite universe' in the priests' theological dialogue is metaphysical speculation, not a material depiction of other planets, dimensions, nonordinary cosmic environments, or visitors from them.

A comet 'that might destroy the world' is mentioned only as a past ruse Flambeau used to escape; it is an incidental reference, not an actual, impending, remembered, or causally central large-scale disaster. The plot concerns a jewel theft.

candidates.description: Valentin's investigative method of deliberately following oddities and the 'unreasonable' when no clue exists, on the theory that whatever anomaly catches the pursuer's eye may be what caught the pursued's.

novelty.rationale: Valentin's method is an unusual detective heuristic, but it introduces no totalizing or world-altering difference from the empirical norm. The storyworld remains ordinary Edwardian London operating under normal physical and social laws; the method is an eccentric procedure, not a novum that changes the universe.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The method is given a coherent, systematic, non-supernatural rationale grounded in experimental psychology and the association of ideas, and is applied methodically (tasting containers, framing questions as inquiry). It is internally consistent and rationalist.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The trail of the unreasonable structures the entire chase plot; the sequence of oddities (salt/sugar, mislabeled fruit, broken window) drives the narrative forward and organizes its logic.

estrangement.rationale: The reader-facing contrast between Valentin's ordinary holiday appearance and his hidden powers, and the detective's and inspector's reactions of disbelief ('Are we after escaped lunatics?'), foreground the strangeness of the method, but this estrangement is of procedure, not of a changed empirical world.

candidates.description: Father Brown's deliberate manufacture of a trail of anomalies (salt/sugar swap, mislabeled produce, overpaid-then-broken window) as a covert signalling and testing device to summon police and unmask Flambeau.

novelty.rationale: This is a clever detective/plot device operating entirely within ordinary empirical reality. No world-altering or totalizing difference from the author's empirical norm is introduced; it is a ruse, not a novum.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The scheme is fully explained through coherent, non-supernatural reasoning: each anomaly is a test of behavior or a means of leaving a talked-about trail, systematically consistent.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The concealed trail is the central engine of the plot and its climactic reveal; the whole narrative logic resolves around it.

estrangement.rationale: The anomalies produce reader-facing bewilderment and character reactions of disbelief, but the estrangement is dissolved by a mundane rational explanation, not by a persistently altered storyworld.
